tables.name: analytics_events

columns.name: id
columns.doc: Auto-incrementing primary key generated by the analytics_events_id_seq sequence.

columns.name: uid
columns.doc: References users.id but is nullable and has no enforced foreign key, so it can point to nonexistent or deleted users.

columns.name: event
columns.doc: Free-text event name with no enum or check constraint, so values are prone to typos and naming drift.

columns.name: props
columns.doc: Schemaless jsonb bag of event-specific properties with no validation, so shape can vary arbitrarily between rows.

columns.name: ts
columns.doc: Bigint epoch timestamp of the event, but the unit (seconds vs milliseconds) is not documented and must be confirmed before use.

tables.doc: analytics_events is a generic event-tracking table capturing user actions (event name + free-form JSON props) with an unenforced link to users via uid; at only ~8 rows and 8 writes/day it appears to be either a new/low-traffic feature or a table not yet fully wired into the app. Engineers must note that ts is a bigint (epoch, unit unconfirmed - seconds vs ms not documented) rather than a timestamp type, and there is no application-level or DB-level constraint on the event column's allowed values.
issues: uid has no enforced foreign key to users, risking orphaned events if users are deleted or uid is mistyped
ts is stored as bigint instead of a timestamp/timestamptz, with no documented unit (seconds vs milliseconds), inviting comparison/conversion bugs
event is an unconstrained free-text field with no enum/check constraint, allowing typos and inconsistent naming to fragment analytics
uid, event, ts, and props are all nullable, so incomplete/garbage events (no user, no name, no time) can be inserted silently
props is schemaless jsonb with no validation, so downstream consumers must defensively handle arbitrary or missing keys
no created_at/updated_at audit columns independent of the business-meaning ts field, making row insertion time unrecoverable if ts is app-supplied and wrong

tables.name: feature_flags

columns.name: flag
columns.doc: Primary key text identifier for the feature flag; must be unique but is unconstrained free text with no naming convention enforced.

columns.name: enabled
columns.doc: Nullable boolean toggle defaulting to false; null should be treated carefully since it is distinct from an explicit false.

columns.name: rollout
columns.doc: Optional JSONB blob holding rollout targeting rules with no enforced schema, so structure may vary or drift undocumented between flags.

tables.doc: A tiny key-value style table used to toggle application features on/off, with an optional JSONB payload for granular rollout rules (e.g., percentage or cohort targeting). At only ~2 rows and minimal read/write volume, this is clearly a hand-maintained config table rather than a high-throughput data store, so treat changes as operational/config changes, not typical app data mutations.
issues: `enabled` is nullable, creating an ambiguous three-state (true/false/null) enum instead of a clean boolean default; consumers must decide how to treat null (as false, or as error).
`rollout` JSONB has no schema/constraint, so its shape (percentage vs cohort vs targeting rules) is undocumented and can drift silently between the two rows.
No `updated_at`/`updated_by` audit columns, making it impossible to trace who last toggled a flag or when, which is risky for a table that gates production behavior.
No relationships/FKs and no enum constraint on `flag` values, so flag names are just free text with no registry enforcing uniqueness of intent or preventing typos creating orphaned/unused flags.

columns.name: order_id
columns.doc: Nullable reference to an order; its enforced FK points to the deprecated 'orders' table rather than the live 'orders_v2', and the correct relationship is unenforced.

columns.name: product_id
columns.doc: Nullable reference to a product with no enforced foreign key, so orphaned or invalid product references are possible.

columns.name: qty

columns.name: unit_price_cents
columns.doc: Nullable integer price in cents (avoids float rounding issues) but lacks a currency field and any non-negativity constraint.

tables.doc: Line-item table capturing product/quantity/price detail for orders, read ~42x/day and currently receiving zero writes and holding zero rows, suggesting it's inactive, unpopulated, or mid-migration. Critical caveat: its enforced FK on order_id points to the deprecated 'orders' table, not the live 'orders_v2' table, so any new writes or joins against current order data will fail or silently reference the wrong table.
issues: order_id has an enforced FK to deprecated 'orders' table instead of live 'orders_v2', making the constraint actively misleading
relationship to orders_v2 (the real live table) is unenforced, so referential integrity for current data is not guaranteed at the DB level
product_id has no enforced FK to products, allowing orphaned references to nonexistent products
order_id and product_id are nullable, permitting line items with no associated order or product
unit_price_cents stores money as an integer with no currency column, risking ambiguity in multi-currency contexts and no enforcement against negative values
qty and unit_price_cents are nullable with no CHECK constraints, allowing zero/negative/NULL quantities or prices
0 rows and 0 writes/day with nonzero reads/day suggests the table may be dead, orphaned, or read by code paths expecting data that no longer arrives

tables.name: orders

columns.name: id
columns.doc: Auto-incrementing primary key generated from orders_id_seq; stable identifier for joins.

columns.name: user_id
columns.doc: References users.id but is nullable, so some orders may have no associated user despite the FK.

columns.name: total
columns.doc: Order total stored as numeric with no currency field or NOT NULL constraint, so NULL totals are possible and units are unspecified.

columns.name: status
columns.doc: Free-text order status with no enum or check constraint, so values may be inconsistent or undocumented across rows.

columns.name: created_at
columns.doc: Defaults to now() on insert but is nullable, so backfilled or manually inserted rows may lack a timestamp.

tables.doc: The `orders` table is a small, low-write, legacy order record (~3 rows, only 3 writes/day) that appears to be superseded by `orders_v2`, since `order_items.order_id` has a broken FK pointing back to this deprecated table instead of the live one. Treat this table as read-mostly/archival; do not build new features against it, and confirm with data owners before trusting `order_items` joins here.
issues: order_items -> orders FK is marked broken/deprecated; live order item data actually lives in orders_v2, risking silent data loss or stale joins if this table is queried as source of truth
user_id is nullable with no visible NOT NULL/FK enforcement details beyond 'enforced: true' claim, so orphaned orders (NULL user_id) are possible and unexplained
total is numeric but nullable with no currency/unit column, so NULL vs 0 vs currency ambiguity is unresolved
status is a free-text column with no enum/check constraint, allowing arbitrary/inconsistent values
created_at is nullable despite having a now() default, meaning historical or backfilled rows could have NULL timestamps
No updated_at column exists, so there's no way to track status changes or edits after order creation

tables.name: orders_v2

columns.name: id
columns.doc: Auto-incrementing bigint primary key generated from orders_v2_id_seq.

columns.name: user_id
columns.doc: Nullable bigint intended as an FK to users, but not enforced at the DB level.

columns.name: workspace_id
columns.doc: Nullable bigint intended as an FK to workspaces, but not enforced at the DB level.

columns.name: amount_cents
columns.doc: Order amount stored as integer cents (not float) but nullable, so missing monetary values are possible.

columns.name: status
columns.doc: Free-text order status defaulting to the undocumented magic value 'p', with no enum or CHECK constraint limiting valid states.

columns.name: meta
columns.doc: Unstructured jsonb bag for arbitrary order metadata with no schema validation.

columns.name: created_at
columns.doc: Timestamptz defaulting to now() at insert time, but nullable so it can be missing on some rows.

tables.doc: orders_v2 is the current orders table (v2 suffix implies a prior orders schema was replaced/migrated, but no migration notes exist) tracking user/workspace purchases with money stored as integer cents. It's low-volume (~17 rows, 41 reads/17 writes per day) and is referenced by order_items and payments, but none of its relationships are enforced by real foreign keys, so referential integrity depends entirely on application code.
issues: No enforced foreign keys to users, workspaces, order_items, or payments — orphaned rows are possible and undetectable at the DB level
status is a free-text column with no CHECK constraint or enum; the default value 'p' is a cryptic, undocumented magic code (presumably 'pending') with no defined set of valid states
user_id and workspace_id are nullable, so it's ambiguous whether an order can legitimately exist without an owner/workspace or if this is just missing data
amount_cents and status are both nullable, allowing orders with unknown/zero monetary value and unknown lifecycle state to be inserted
meta jsonb column is unconstrained/schemaless, inviting inconsistent or undocumented ad-hoc fields over time
'_v2' naming suggests a prior 'orders' table exists or existed; no documentation of what changed or whether the old table/data was fully migrated or is still referenced elsewhere
created_at is nullable despite having a now() default, so backfilled or bypassed inserts could leave it null, breaking chronological assumptions

tables.name: payments

columns.name: order_id

columns.name: stripe_event_id

columns.name: amount_cents

columns.name: state

columns.name: created_at

tables.doc: Stores Stripe payment records linked to orders (via unenforced FK to orders_v2), used to reconcile payment state against order fulfillment. Table is tiny (~11 rows) with low write volume, suggesting it's either new, a test/staging table, or payments for a low-traffic system. The 'orders_v2' naming signals a prior schema migration that engineers should be aware of when tracing lineage.
issues: order_id has no enforced foreign key to orders_v2, risking orphaned payment records
order_id, amount_cents, state, and created_at are all nullable despite being core fields for a payments table
state is an unconstrained free-text enum with no CHECK constraint, allowing typos/inconsistent values
amount_cents stored as integer is fine for cents, but lack of a currency column is risky if multi-currency support is ever added
stripe_event_id is nullable and has no unique constraint, so duplicate Stripe webhook events could create duplicate payment rows
no updated_at column to track state transitions (e.g., pending -> succeeded -> refunded)
table name 'orders_v2' suggests a legacy 'orders' table may still exist, risking confusion about which is authoritative

columns.name: name

columns.name: price
columns.doc: Product price stored as double precision (float), which can introduce rounding/precision errors for currency values.

columns.name: cat
columns.doc: Abbreviated, unconstrained category label with no foreign key or enum backing it, inviting inconsistent values.

tables.doc: Legacy product catalog table (note the 'old' suffix and near-zero activity: 1 row, 0 reads/day, 1 write/day) that appears to be an abandoned or deprecated precursor to a current product_catalog table. No primary key, no constraints, and no relationships are defined, so it should not be treated as a source of truth; confirm with the team whether this can be archived or dropped.
issues: No primary key defined on the table (pid is not marked primaryKey), so uniqueness of products is not enforced
All columns are nullable with no defaults, allowing fully empty rows
price stored as double precision (float) instead of a fixed-point/numeric/decimal type, risking rounding errors in monetary values
'cat' is an unconstrained free-text/abbreviated column with no enum, lookup table, or foreign key, risking inconsistent category naming
No relationships/foreign keys defined despite 'cat' implying a category reference
Table name suggests deprecation ('_old' suffix) but no formal deprecation status, owner, or migration path is documented

tables.doc: Stores the product catalog (currently tiny, ~4 rows) used to look up SKU, title, and price for order line items; order_items.product_id references this table but the FK is not DB-enforced, so referential integrity relies entirely on application logic. Price is stored as integer cents (good practice), but almost every other column is nullable with no constraints, so bad data can slip in silently.
issues: order_items -> products relationship via product_id is not enforced at the DB level, allowing orphaned line items or references to deleted/nonexistent products
sku is nullable and has no unique constraint, so duplicate or missing SKUs are possible despite SKU typically being a natural business key
title, price_cents, and active are all nullable with no defaults (except active), risking incomplete product records (e.g. null price treated as $0 or causing calculation errors downstream)
active has no enforced boolean-only usage risk but combined with no soft-delete audit trail (no updated_at/deactivated_at), there's no way to track when/why a product was deactivated
created_at is nullable despite having a now() default, so it can be explicitly set to null bypassing the default
no updated_at column, making it impossible to audit changes to price, title, or active status over time

tables.doc: Stores active user session tokens for authentication, keyed by opaque token string, with an expiry timestamp and enforced FK to users.id. issues: user_id and expires_at are both nullable despite being essential for session validity — a null expires_at implies a session that never expires, and a null user_id implies an orphaned/anonymous session with no clear semantics.

Zero writes/day with 0 rows but nonzero reads/day is suspicious: either the write path bypasses this table (e.g., sessions stored elsewhere like Redis/JWT) or this table is dead/deprecated code still being polled.

columns.name: received_at

tables.doc: Stores raw Stripe webhook event payloads as they're received, keyed by Stripe's event id (used implicitly for idempotency/dedup on insert). At ~5 rows and 5 writes/day with almost no reads, this looks like a low-volume or early-stage integration table, likely intended as an audit/replay log rather than a queryable operational table.
issues: No event_type/status column, so consumers must parse the jsonb payload to know what kind of event occurred or whether it's been processed — no way to track processing state or retries.
received_at is nullable despite defaulting to now(); a null here would be ambiguous (backfilled row? failed insert?) and breaks chronological ordering guarantees.
payload is nullable, meaning a row could exist with no actual event data, which is meaningless for an event log.

No foreign keys or relationships at all — table is fully orphaned from the rest of the schema, so there's no way to trace a Stripe event to the internal entity (customer, invoice, subscription) it affected.
id is text with no documented format/constraint — nothing enforces it's actually a valid Stripe event id (e.g. 'evt_...'), risking silent duplicate or malformed inserts.
No processed_at/handled flag, so this table can't distinguish between events that were successfully acted upon versus just logged.
